The month most travelers assume is the worst time to eat in Turkey produces the best evenings of the Turkish year. For thirty days the country runs on a different clock, and if you happen to be there, the food side of it is worth understanding rather than avoiding.

Here is how Turkish restaurants, bakeries and hotels actually run during Ramadan, and what appears on tables that isn't there any other month.

The clock everything runs on

Iftar begins at the local Maghrib prayer time — sunset — published daily by Diyanet for each location, and the time advances by a few minutes each day as the month progresses.

Two things follow that matter practically. Iftar is a moment, not a service window: a restaurant serving iftar starts at the minute, not "around seven". And because it tracks sunset, it differs across the country on the same evening — Istanbul and the far east of Turkey break fast noticeably apart.

The published local timetable is called an imsakiye, and it lists both ends of the day: imsak before dawn, iftar at sunset.

Eating out at iftar

Restaurants offering iftar typically serve a set menu — often a fixed multi-course or buffet — timed to the call to prayer, and many take advance bookings, particularly in larger cities.

The atmosphere is the point. Tables are laid before sunset with the traditional openers already out — dates, olives, soup, pide — and nobody touches anything until the call. Then the room starts at once. It is the single most convivial hour in a Turkish city, and non-fasting visitors are entirely welcome at it.

The practical corollary is that the hour before sunset is the quietest a restaurant will ever be, and the hour after is the busiest.

The bread, and the queue

Ramazan pidesi — a round, sesame-topped flatbread — and güllaç appear seasonally during the month and are sold by bakeries and pastry shops.

Ramazan pidesi exists only in Ramadan and is baked in batches timed to come out shortly before sunset, which produces the most recognisable street scene of the month: a line outside a bakery in the late afternoon, lengthening as the hour approaches. The bread is sold warm and is gone quickly. You don't need to be fasting to join the queue, and it is one of the easier ways to feel like you're in the country rather than beside it.

Güllaç is the month's dessert — thin sheets of starch pastry soaked in rosewater milk, layered with walnuts, and lighter than almost anything else in the Turkish sweet repertoire. It appears in patisseries for the month and disappears afterwards.

Sahur, the other meal

Sahur, the pre-dawn meal, is usually eaten at home, though some hotels and 24-hour restaurants offer sahur menus, with availability highest in the major cities and tourist hotels and more limited in smaller towns.

In some neighbourhoods you'll also hear the Ramadan drummer walking the streets before dawn to wake households for it — a tradition that survives in residential districts and has largely gone from tourist ones. Whether you experience it depends entirely on where you're sleeping.

Daytime, and where you are

Observed practice is that some restaurants and cafés reduce or suspend daytime service during Ramadan, particularly away from tourist areas; in the major cities and coastal resorts many stay open through the day, and in smaller inland towns daytime options can be genuinely limited.

Nothing about this is regulated — each business decides. Lunch in Beyoğlu or Kaleiçi during Ramadan is unremarkable. Lunch in a small central-Anatolian town can mean a bakery and a shop rather than a restaurant. Hotel breakfast is unaffected everywhere.

The broader picture of what changes during the month, and what's expected of a visitor, is in Ramadan in Turkey: what actually changes.

When Ramadan falls, and how its dates sit against the months a trip is usually planned for, connects to the seasonal picture rather than the food one. Turkey, Worked Out puts those together.

FAQ

What time is iftar?

At the local Maghrib (sunset) prayer time, published daily by Diyanet for each location, moving by a few minutes each day. It differs across the country on the same evening, so use the local timetable.

Can non-Muslims eat iftar at a restaurant?

Yes, and it's one of the better meals of the Turkish year. Set menus timed to the call to prayer are common, and larger cities often take advance bookings.

Can I get lunch during Ramadan?

In tourist areas and big cities, generally yes. Some places reduce or suspend daytime service, mostly away from tourist areas, and inland towns can be genuinely limited. It varies by business, not by rule.

What is Ramazan pidesi?

A round sesame-topped flatbread baked only during Ramadan, timed to come out shortly before sunset — hence the late-afternoon bakery queues. It and güllaç appear seasonally and are sold by bakeries and pastry shops.

Is breakfast still served at hotels?

Yes. Hotel breakfast runs normally throughout the month everywhere, including in areas where daytime restaurant service thins out.

Turkey's two biggest holidays are not on the Gregorian calendar, don't fall on the same dates twice, and between them account for the only weeks of the year when the whole country is trying to travel at once. Americans planning around Turkish dates routinely find the national holidays and miss these two entirely.

Here is what each one is, how long it officially lasts, and where it lands next.

The two Bayrams

Ramazan Bayramı

The three-day festival that ends the fasting month — Eid al-Fitr elsewhere, and colloquially Şeker Bayramı, the "sugar holiday", for the sweets given to visiting children. It falls immediately after Ramadan, so it inherits Ramadan's movement through the calendar.

The next one runs 9-11 March 2027, preceded by a half-day from 13:00 on 8 March.

Kurban Bayramı

The Feast of Sacrifice — Eid al-Adha — and the larger of the two, both in length and in how much the country moves. The next one runs 16-19 May 2027, preceded by a half-day from 13:00 on 15 May.

How long they officially last

This is set in law rather than by custom, and the structure is the same for both: a half-day first, then the full days.

The arife — the eve — of each religious Bayram is a half-day public holiday beginning at 13:00, when official institutions and many workplaces close. Ramazan Bayramı then runs three full days; Kurban Bayramı runs four.

So the official block is three and a half days for the first and four and a half for the second, and the half-day is the part visitors miss. A bank open at 11am on the eve is closed at 2pm.

The gap between them

About two lunar months separate the two Bayrams; in 2026 and 2027 the interval works out around 66 to 70 days. Because both are pinned to the lunar calendar, the gap is roughly fixed while the pair as a whole drifts earlier each year.

The drift, and what it collides with

Both Bayrams move backwards through the Gregorian year at the same rate as Ramadan — roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.

That matters more than it first sounds, because it means the seasons each Bayram lands in change. Kurban Bayramı currently falls in the second half of May, drifting into early May, then late April, over the next few years. Ramazan Bayramı is currently in March, drifting into February.

Anyone who checked Turkish holiday dates on a previous trip and assumed they'd repeat is working from a calendar that has already moved.

What is legally closed

Banks, government offices and official institutions close on all national public holidays and on the full days of both Bayrams, plus the arife half-day from 13:00.

Commercial life is a different matter and follows no single rule — shops, restaurants and tourist businesses make their own decisions, and those decisions differ between a coastal resort in season and an inland town. Istanbul's Grand Bazaar closes on Sundays and on the first day of religious Bayrams, which is its own long-standing rule rather than a general one.

The extras nobody can predict

Two things routinely happen around Bayram that are decided year by year rather than fixed in advance.

Turkey does not automatically extend Bayram with bridge days; additional administrative leave for public-sector employees may be announced by decision on a year-by-year basis and published when decided. Some years the holiday is effectively longer than the legal block. Some years it isn't.

The other is transport. Toll-free passage over Bayram is not automatic: it is granted by a presidential decree published in the Official Gazette for that year's holiday window, and when granted it covers bridges and motorways operated by the General Directorate of Highways plus free municipal public transport, while excluding build-operate-transfer crossings such as the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge.

Both are announced rather than scheduled, which is the practical point: the legal holiday can be looked up years ahead, and the extras cannot be looked up at all until that year's announcement.

The machinery behind all of this — who declares what, and when — is set out in how Turkey's holiday calendar is actually set.

Where these dates fall against the months a first trip is usually planned for is a question that runs across the seasonal guides rather than sitting inside any one of them. Turkey, Worked Out maps the calendar against the seasons in one place.

FAQ

What are the two Bayrams?

Ramazan Bayramı, the three-day festival ending the fasting month, and Kurban Bayramı, the four-day Feast of Sacrifice about two months later. Both are national public holidays fixed in law.

When is the next Bayram?

Ramazan Bayramı falls 9-11 March 2027, preceded by a half-day from 13:00 on 8 March, and Kurban Bayramı 16-19 May 2027, preceded by a half-day from 13:00 on 15 May.

How long is the official holiday?

The eve is a half-day from 13:00, then three full days for Ramazan Bayramı and four for Kurban Bayramı — three and a half and four and a half days in total.

Do the dates change every year?

Yes. Both move about 10 to 11 days earlier each Gregorian year, because they follow the lunar calendar. Dates from a previous trip won't repeat.

Is everything closed during Bayram?

Banks, government offices and official institutions close for the full days and the arife half-day. Shops, restaurants and tourist businesses follow no single rule and vary by region.

Turkish export law is only half the journey. The other half is what US customs does when you land, and it has its own restrictions, its own paperwork, and one rule aimed specifically at Turkey that almost no traveler knows exists.

Here's the American side of the same purchase.

The personal exemption

Returning US residents may bring back goods acquired abroad for personal or household use up to an aggregate fair retail value of $800 duty-free, provided the goods accompany the traveller, the stay abroad was at least 48 hours, and the exemption hasn't been used within the preceding 30 days.

Four conditions, and each one does work. The value is aggregate, not per item. The goods must travel with you — anything shipped separately sits outside the exemption. The 48-hour minimum rules out short trips. And the 30-day rule catches frequent travelers.

Above $800, ordinary duty applies. That is a cost, not a prohibition.

Declaration is not optional

All articles acquired abroad must be declared. Failure to declare items that should be declared risks forfeiture, and the exemption applies only to declared accompanying goods that meet the statutory conditions.

Note the second half. The exemption isn't a threshold below which nothing needs saying — it's a relief that applies to goods you have declared. Undeclared goods don't qualify for it, which inverts the intuition that staying under $800 means staying quiet.

The rule aimed at Turkey

This is the one worth knowing about, because it's specific and it's current.

The United States maintains import restrictions on designated categories of archaeological material — approximately 1.2 million BC to AD 1770 — and ethnological material from the 1st century AD to 1923, from Türkiye, under a bilateral memorandum implementing the 1970 UNESCO Convention. The restrictions were extended through 24 March 2031.

Two things stand out. The ethnological window runs to 1923, which is far more recent than "antiquity" suggests and reaches ordinary-looking Ottoman-era objects. And this is a US restriction operating independently of Turkish law — an object can clear Turkish departure and still meet a restricted description on arrival.

The two systems aren't mirrors of each other. Clearing one says nothing about the other.

Everyday purchases

Most commercially packaged food products and textiles for personal use are admissible subject to ordinary agricultural and textile rules; certain meats, plants and soil are prohibited or restricted, and textiles may face quota or labelling requirements in commercial quantities.

For the things people actually carry home from Turkey — sealed Turkish delight, packaged tea and spices, soap, ceramics, textiles — this is unremarkable. The agricultural restrictions bite on fresh produce, meat, seeds and anything with soil attached, which is a different shopping list.

Sealed and commercially packaged is the pattern that travels. Loose, fresh, or agricultural is the pattern that doesn't.

Documentation for something expensive

For high-value personal imports, customs expects a sales receipt or invoice showing description, purchase price and date, and, where cultural-property restrictions may apply, proof that the object is not on the designated list or was lawfully exported from Türkiye.

The second half of that only engages for objects near the restricted categories. But it's worth reading carefully: the proof contemplated is either that the object falls outside the list, or that it left Turkey lawfully — which loops directly back to the Turkish determination discussed in what Turkish law protects.

For an ordinary purchase, the receipt is the whole of it. For an object with age, the two jurisdictions start asking each other's questions.

How the two systems sit together

Worth being explicit, because travelers routinely assume one clearance implies the other:

  • Turkey asks whether the object may leave, on criteria assessed by a state museum.
  • The United States asks whether the object may enter, against a designated list defined by date ranges and material type.
  • Neither defers to the other, and the date ranges in the US list don't correspond to anything in Turkish law, which sets no age threshold at all.

An object can be unremarkable under one and described by the other. That's not a contradiction — they're answering different questions on different criteria.

Holding both systems in view at the moment of purchase, rather than discovering the second one at a baggage hall, is exactly what these guides can supply the parts for but not do. Turkey, Worked Out does it.

FAQ

How much can I bring back duty-free?

An aggregate $800 of accompanying goods, if you were abroad at least 48 hours and haven't used the exemption within 30 days. Shipped goods don't accompany you.

Do I have to declare things under $800?

Yes. All articles acquired abroad must be declared, and the exemption applies only to declared goods — staying under the figure isn't a reason to stay quiet.

Does the US restrict Turkish antiques specifically?

Yes. Import restrictions cover designated archaeological material and ethnological material from the 1st century AD to 1923, extended through 24 March 2031. The 1923 end-date reaches ordinary-looking Ottoman-era objects.

Can I bring Turkish delight and spices home?

Commercially packaged foods and textiles for personal use are generally admissible; meats, plants and soil are restricted or prohibited. Sealed and packaged travels; fresh and agricultural doesn't.

If Turkey let it out, will the US let it in?

Not necessarily. The two systems ask different questions on different criteria and neither defers to the other — the US list is defined by date ranges, while Turkish law sets no age threshold at all.

Turkish holiday dates come from three different places, and understanding which one produces which piece explains something travelers find genuinely confusing: why some Turkish holidays can be looked up a decade ahead, others only a year ahead, and some not until a few weeks before they happen.

Three authorities, three kinds of certainty.

One: the law fixes the dates that don't move

Turkey's national holidays are set by statute, which is why they never shift. The fixed public holidays are 1 January, 23 April, 1 May, 19 May, 15 July, 30 August and 29 October, with a half-day from 13:00 on 28 October.

These are the certainties. You can plan against them for any year you like.

Two: the law fixes the length of the religious holidays, but not their position

This is the part that surprises people. The two Bayrams are national public holidays with a legally defined duration — the statute says how long, and the lunar calendar says when.

The eve of each religious Bayram is a half-day public holiday beginning at 13:00, when official institutions and many workplaces close, and the full days follow: three for Ramazan Bayramı, four for Kurban Bayramı.

So the shape of the holiday is permanent and the position is not. That's an unusual combination for anyone used to holidays that are either fixed (Christmas) or fixed-by-rule (fourth Thursday in November).

Three: Diyanet declares the religious dates

The Presidency of Religious Affairs — Diyanet — publishes the religious calendar, including Ramadan and both Bayrams. Its calendar is what Turkish institutions, employers and transport operators work from.

The dates are calculated astronomically and published well in advance, which is why you can find 8 February to 8 March 2027 for the next Ramadan today. But they remain subject to confirmation against the lunar month, so a date printed a year ahead can move by a day. A published Turkish religious date is a strong forecast rather than a fixture, and the honest way to read one is as provisional until close to the time.

Why they move at all

The Islamic lunar calendar is about eleven days shorter than the solar Gregorian year, so Ramadan and both Bayrams fall roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each Gregorian year. Over about three decades each one travels through every season and returns.

The practical consequence is that Turkish holiday dates don't repeat. Notes from a previous trip, or a friend's advice from three years ago, describe a calendar that has already moved by a month.

The third layer: what gets decided each year

On top of the statutory holiday, some things are decided annually by government decision and cannot be known in advance at all.

Extra administrative leave

Turkey does not automatically extend Bayram with bridge days; additional administrative leave for public-sector employees may be announced on a year-by-year basis and published when decided. In some years a four-and-a-half-day legal block becomes a longer effective one. In others it doesn't.

Toll-free travel

Toll-free passage over Bayram is not automatic: it is granted by a presidential decree published in the Official Gazette for that year's holiday window, and when granted it covers bridges and motorways operated by the General Directorate of Highways plus free municipal public transport, while excluding build-operate-transfer crossings such as the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge.

The exclusion is the detail worth keeping. Even in a year when the decree is issued, not every crossing is covered — the BOT bridges and motorways charge as usual, which for a driver in Istanbul means one Bosphorus crossing may be free while another isn't.

Reading a Turkish date, in short

Three questions answer almost everything:

  • Is it a fixed national holiday? Then it's in the statute and it's certain.
  • Is it a religious holiday? Then its length is in the statute and its date comes from Diyanet, provisional until confirmed.
  • Is it extra leave or free tolls? Then it's a government decision for that year and it doesn't exist until announced.

The dates themselves are in the guide to the two Bayram holidays, and the closures in what closes on a Turkish public holiday.

What none of these pages does is put the moving calendar against the seasons a trip is actually planned for. Turkey, Worked Out does that in one place.

FAQ

Who decides Turkish holiday dates?

Three authorities. Statute fixes the national holidays and the length of the religious ones, Diyanet declares the religious dates, and a government decision each year adds anything extra such as administrative leave or toll-free travel.

Why do Turkish holidays move?

The lunar calendar is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, so the religious holidays fall roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each Gregorian year. The fixed national holidays don't move at all.

How far ahead can I look up a Bayram date?

Diyanet publishes years in advance and the calculation is astronomical, but confirmation against the lunar month means a date can shift by a day. Treat a distant date as provisional rather than fixed.

Are the tolls free during Bayram?

Only when a decree says so that year. When granted it covers General Directorate of Highways bridges and motorways plus free municipal transport, and excludes build-operate-transfer crossings such as the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge.

Will the Bayram holiday be extended this year?

Not knowable ahead of the announcement. There are no automatic bridge days; extra administrative leave is announced year by year when decided.

Turkey has two kinds of public holiday and they behave completely differently. The religious ones move about eleven days earlier each year. The national ones sit on fixed dates and never move — and those are the ones an American planning a trip is most likely to walk into unaware, because none of them coincides with a US holiday.

Here is the fixed calendar, what legally closes on those days, and what doesn't.

The fixed national holidays

Turkey's fixed public holidays are 1 January (New Year), 23 April (National Sovereignty and Children's Day), 1 May (Labour and Solidarity Day), 19 May (Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day), 15 July (Democracy and National Unity Day), 30 August (Victory Day), and 29 October (Republic Day), which is preceded by a half-day from 13:00 on 28 October.

Two of those are worth a second look for anyone travelling in spring. The 23 April and 19 May holidays fall inside the window most first trips are planned for, and Republic Day on 29 October sits at the end of it. None of them stops a holiday, but all of them close the official half of the country.

The half-day pattern

Republic Day carries the same structure as the religious Bayrams: a half-day from 13:00 the afternoon before, then the full day. The eve of each religious Bayram is likewise a half-day public holiday from 13:00, when official institutions and many workplaces close.

The half-day is the part that catches people. An office or bank you could use in the morning is shut after lunch, and the closure is legal rather than discretionary.

What closes, legally

Banks, government offices and official institutions are closed on all national public holidays and on the full days of both Bayrams, plus the arife half-day from 13:00.

That's the whole of the legal closure, and for a traveler it means a specific short list: no banking counter, no government office, no post office. Card payments, ATMs and everything online continue as normal.

What follows its own rule

Istanbul's covered bazaars are the notable exception to the general commercial pattern. The Grand Bazaar closes on Sundays and on the first day of religious Bayrams — a long-standing rule of its own rather than a consequence of the public-holiday law.

That combination is worth noticing: a Sunday that also falls on a Bayram is not doubly closed, but a Bayram that falls midweek closes the bazaar on a day it would normally be busy.

What the public-holiday law doesn't reach

Shops, restaurants, hotels and tourist businesses aren't covered by the closure rule and make their own decisions. There is no national pattern to report — practice differs between a resort town in season, a big-city tourist district and a small inland town, and it differs between one business and the one next door.

The same is true of museums and archaeological sites: no single published schedule sets their holiday hours, and they are handled site by site. If a specific site matters to your plan on a specific date, its own page is the only reliable source.

National holidays versus Bayram

The two kinds of holiday feel different on the ground even though the legal closure is identical.

A fixed national holiday is a day off. Ceremonies, flags, a public mood, and everything commercial running more or less normally. The religious Bayrams are longer blocks — a half-day from 13:00 and then three or four full days — and they carry a family-visiting tradition that a single day off doesn't.

They're covered separately in the guide to the two Bayram holidays, and the machinery that sets both is in how Turkey's holiday calendar is actually set.

Which of these dates a trip actually runs into depends on the months it's planned for, and that connection is made across the seasonal guides rather than inside any one of them. Turkey, Worked Out puts the calendar and the seasons side by side.

FAQ

What are Turkey's public holidays?

1 January, 23 April, 1 May, 19 May, 15 July, 30 August and 29 October, with a half-day from 13:00 on 28 October, plus the two religious Bayrams, which move each year.

Will banks be open?

Banks, government offices and official institutions close on national holidays and on the full days of both Bayrams, plus the arife half-day from 13:00. ATMs and card payments are unaffected.

Is the Grand Bazaar open on a holiday?

It closes on Sundays and on the first day of religious Bayrams — its own rule, separate from the public-holiday law.

Do museums and sites close?

There's no single published schedule covering holiday hours across state museums and sites; it's handled individually. For a specific site on a specific date, check that site's own page.

What's the half-day rule?

The afternoon before Republic Day and before each religious Bayram is a half-day holiday from 13:00. Somewhere open in the morning may be closed after lunch, and that closure is legal rather than discretionary.

A rug is the purchase most American visitors to Turkey actually consider, and the one where the amounts get serious. It's also where two separate legal systems meet a piece of wool: what Turkey allows out, and what the United States lets in.

Neither question is about rugs specifically, which is part of why the answers are hard to find.

Turkish law doesn't have a carpet rule

Buyers look for a threshold — an age above which a rug can't leave. There isn't one written for textiles.

Carpets and kilims fall under the same criteria as any other movable cultural property: protection attaches if they meet the historic-period and scientific-or-cultural-value tests in the statute, regardless of trade age-band terminology.

And the statute sets no fixed numerical age or cut-off date for movable cultural property — protection attaches to objects of prehistoric or historic periods possessing the statutory criteria.

So a rug is assessed exactly as a coin or an icon would be, on character and value rather than on a birthday. The full framework, including what unauthorised export carries, is in what Turkish law protects.

The trade's vocabulary isn't the law's

The rug trade speaks in bands — new, semi-old, old, antique — and those terms do real work in a shop. They describe condition, technique, dye, market. What they don't do is map onto the statute, which contains no textile category and no age band at all.

A dealer calling a piece "semi-antique" is pricing it, not classifying it.

Shipping or carrying

Buyers frequently ask whether it's safer to have the shop ship it. The honest answer is that no official source distinguishes the two routes.

Nothing in the primary law creates a separate documentation regime for freight versus luggage, and neither does anything published about the process. The obligation attaches to the object, not to the method of moving it — a protected object is protected in a crate as much as in a suitcase.

What does differ is who is holding it when a question is asked, and who has the documents. Carrying it yourself means you are present at departure with whatever paperwork exists. Shipping means the object travels under the shop's arrangements, and the documentation trail is theirs to create — which matters given how little standing a shop's own paperwork has, as covered in what a seller's certificate actually proves.

The American side

Returning US residents may bring back goods acquired abroad for personal or household use up to an aggregate fair retail value of $800 duty-free, provided the goods accompany the traveller, the stay abroad was at least 48 hours, and the exemption hasn't been used within the preceding 30 days.

Three conditions there, not one, and the accompaniment condition is the one that interacts with shipping: goods sent separately don't accompany you.

All articles acquired abroad must be declared. Failure to declare items that should be declared risks forfeiture, and the exemption applies only to declared accompanying goods meeting the statutory conditions.

A personal-use rug acquired in Turkey is treated as an ordinary commercial good for duty purposes and may fall within the personal exemption if it qualifies; it is not automatically subject to the cultural-property restrictions unless it falls within the restricted archaeological or ethnological categories.

That last clause is the hinge. An ordinary rug is an ordinary import. A rug that meets the restricted description is a different matter entirely, and that's covered in bringing Turkish purchases into the United States.

What you're holding at each stage

It helps to see the documents as a sequence rather than a bundle.

  • At purchase — a receipt, which establishes ownership and price, and possibly a shop certificate, which establishes neither's legal effect.
  • At Turkish departure — whatever determines the object's status under Turkish law, which a shop cannot issue.
  • At US entry — the declaration, where customs expects a sales receipt or invoice showing description, purchase price and date, and, where cultural-property restrictions may apply, proof that the object is not on the restricted list or was lawfully exported.

The receipt is the only document that does work at both ends. It is also the one buyers most often leave behind.

The part that isn't legal at all

Everything above concerns objects near the statutory line. The overwhelming majority of rugs sold to visitors are contemporary pieces that engage none of it — newly manufactured goods without historic or scientific cultural value fall outside the export prohibition entirely.

For those, the whole question collapses into the American one: declare it, keep the receipt, and know where the exemption sits.

Deciding whether the piece you want is worth the question at all — and what to establish before paying rather than after — is exactly what these guides can't settle for you. Turkey, Worked Out settles it.

FAQ

Can I take an old Turkish rug home?

It depends on whether it meets the statutory criteria, not on its age. Carpets fall under the same tests as any other movable cultural property, regardless of trade age-band terminology.

Is there an age limit for carpets?

No. No fixed age or cut-off date is stated for movable cultural property — the trade's bands are commercial vocabulary with no statutory standing.

Is it safer to have the shop ship it?

No official source distinguishes shipping from carrying. The obligation attaches to the object rather than the route. What changes is who holds it and who creates the paperwork.

Will I pay US duty?

Up to $800 of accompanying goods is duty-free if you were abroad at least 48 hours and haven't used the exemption in 30 days. Above that, ordinary duty applies — a rug is treated as a normal good.

What should I keep?

The receipt. US customs expects an invoice showing description, price and date for a high-value personal import, and it's the only document that does work at both ends of the trip.

Take money out of a Turkish ATM and the amount that leaves your account is not the amount that appears on the screen. Three or four separate charges are applied by three or four separate parties, none of whom mentions the others, and one of them is far larger than most travelers imagine.

Here is what each layer is and who applies it.

The Turkish bank's charge

This is the layer that surprises people, because in most of the world it's a small flat fee.

Akbank publishes a fee for withdrawals by foreign cards at its domestic ATMs of 12.50% to 25.00%, excluding banking transaction tax. Other major Turkish banks' published ATM tariffs primarily cover Turkish cards, and no uniform national foreign-card operator fee is published.

Read that as a percentage, because it is one. Not a flat charge, not a couple of dollars — a proportion of whatever you withdraw, published on the bank's own tariff page.

Two caveats matter. That figure is what one major bank publishes, not a national rate; other banks' pages don't state an equivalent foreign-card surcharge at all, which is not the same as saying they don't charge one. And it excludes the banking transaction tax applied on top.

What follows structurally is that the Turkish layer scales with the amount, while the layers below it mostly don't. Those two behave differently as the withdrawal changes size, and that difference is the whole arithmetic.

Your own bank's charge

US issuing banks commonly apply a fixed per-withdrawal fee and/or a percentage foreign-transaction fee on cash withdrawals abroad, with the exact structure set by each issuer.

No figure appears here because there isn't one to give — this is per-issuer, it changes without notice, and it's the one layer you can establish exactly before leaving, from your own account terms.

The structural point is the same as above: a fixed fee behaves one way against withdrawal size and a percentage behaves another. Which one your issuer uses, or whether it uses both, determines how its charge moves.

The exchange rate itself

The exchange rate applied to a card withdrawal is set by the card network and/or the issuing bank, is separate from any ATM operator fee, and appears as a markup over the wholesale rate.

This is a cost even though it never appears as a line item. It's embedded in the rate, which is why a withdrawal can look fee-free and still be expensive.

The fourth layer, which is optional

Dynamic currency conversion is offered at some Turkish ATMs and card terminals: the machine presents a choice of billing in local currency or your home currency, with the conversion rate set by the DCC provider rather than your card issuer.

Accepting it substitutes the machine's rate for your issuer's. Turkey's currency handling generally is covered in the site's money guide; what's worth registering here is simply that this is a distinct fourth layer, presented as a convenience, applied by a party you have no relationship with.

Limits, and how they interact

Per-withdrawal and daily cash limits at Turkish ATMs vary by bank and card type; foreign card limits are often lower than domestic ones and are set by the issuing bank.

That's observed practice rather than a published rule, and no official source states limits for foreign cards. It matters because a limit interacts with the fee structure: where a charge is fixed, the number of transactions determines the total; where it's a percentage, the number of transactions is irrelevant and the amount is everything.

With a percentage charge on one side and possibly a fixed charge on the other, those two forces don't point the same way.

Putting the layers side by side

A single withdrawal can engage all of these:

  • The Turkish operator — potentially a percentage, published by at least one major bank in double digits.
  • Your issuer's fee — fixed, percentage, or both, knowable in advance from your own terms.
  • The exchange margin — embedded in the rate, invisible as a line.

Here's where cards work, where they don't, and what varies.

Where cards work reliably

Card payment is reliably accepted at hotels, larger restaurants, supermarkets, shopping malls and tourist shops in major cities, with Visa and Mastercard both widely taken; acceptance thins out at small shops, street vendors, public transport and in rural areas.

Bargaining is the clearest case. A negotiated price and a card terminal don't fit together comfortably, and in a bazaar the negotiation is the transaction rather than a preliminary to it.

Tipping is the other consistent one, and it catches Americans specifically, because adding a tip to a card slip is so routine at home that its absence isn't noticed until the moment it's needed.

Card acceptance is most widespread in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir and in resort areas such as Antalya and Cappadocia; in smaller towns and rural areas cash is more dominant.

The pattern maps onto the tourist trail rather than onto wealth. A resort town with a fraction of Ankara's population may be more card-friendly than an ordinary provincial city, because its businesses are built around visitors.

Which means the transition isn't gradual as you travel — it's abrupt, and it happens when you step off the trail rather than as you move further from a city.

Common causes of a foreign card being declined in Turkey include insufficient funds, hitting a daily withdrawal limit, an issuer's fraud detection responding to an unusual location, an incorrect PIN, network problems, or the card not being enabled for international use.

Note that most of those originate at your own bank rather than in Turkey. A decline in a Turkish shop is frequently a decision made in the United States, which is why it can look inexplicable from where you're standing — and why it's covered separately in what freezes a card.

Machines and terminals in Turkey are modern and the networks are reliable. The failure point is usually the relationship between your card and its issuer, not the infrastructure in front of you.

An ATM is not the only way to end up holding lira, and for anyone arriving with dollars it isn't necessarily the obvious one. Turkey has a dense network of licensed exchange offices, bank counters that will do the same job, and a set of customs rules on carrying cash that most travelers get backwards.

How an exchange office works

Licensed exchange offices display separate buying and selling rates, and the spread is the difference between the two. Commission practice varies by office and is not uniformly prohibited or required by a single published rule.

The two-rate display is the mechanism worth understanding, because it's where the cost lives. An office buying dollars at one rate and selling them at another earns the gap, and that gap is the price of the transaction whether or not anything is called a fee.

Which means "no commission" — a common sign — describes only one of two possible charges. A wide spread with no commission can cost more than a narrow spread with one.

How the spread compares between offices, or between an office and an ATM, isn't published anywhere. No official comparative data exists, and any general claim about which is better would be an assertion rather than a fact.

Bank counters and airports

Banks perform the same function, and what a Turkish bank counter asks of a foreign customer isn't documented in any official source — no uniform list of required documents was found. In practice a passport is the baseline expectation for an identified transaction anywhere.

The airport-versus-city question is the same story. There's no official comparative rate table, so the widely repeated claim that airport rates are worse is folk knowledge rather than a published fact. What can be said structurally is that airport exchange operates under different conditions from city exchange — captive demand, higher costs, limited competition — and that those conditions are the kind that generally shape a spread.

That's a mechanism, not a measurement, and it's worth being clear which one it is.

Bringing cash in — the rule everyone reverses

This is the part most travelers have the wrong way round, and it's worth reading carefully.

Import of foreign currency into Turkey is free. For export — taking cash out — amounts exceeding 10,000 euros or equivalent in foreign currency, or exceeding 185,000 Turkish lira, must be declared to customs on the official cash declaration form.

Coming in: no limit, nothing to declare. Going out: a threshold, and a form.

The reversed version — that you must declare above ten thousand on arrival — circulates widely and is stated confidently in plenty of travel writing. It describes the rule in the wrong direction, and the direction is the whole substance of it.

Two separate thresholds also apply, one for foreign currency and a different one for lira, so a mixed holding is measured against both.

Leftover lira

Turkish lira may be taken out of Turkey subject to the same declaration threshold — above 185,000 lira requires declaration — and conversion back to foreign currency is available at banks and licensed exchange offices.

So there's no prohibition on leaving with lira, and no requirement to convert before departing. For ordinary amounts the question is purely practical: lira is not readily exchangeable outside Turkey and its value against the dollar moves, which makes leftover notes a currency position rather than a souvenir.

Converting back engages the same spread as converting in, from the other side.

The choice, laid out

Three routes to holding lira, with genuinely different cost structures:

  • An ATM — where the Turkish operator's charge can be a percentage, as covered in what a Turkish ATM withdrawal actually costs, stacked with your issuer's fee and the exchange margin.
  • An exchange office — where the cost is the spread, possibly plus commission, and where you must already be holding dollars.
  • A bank counter — the same transaction with an identification step and, in practice, opening hours.

Each has a different shape, and the first two respond differently to the amount involved. Carrying dollars in to exchange also has a cost that doesn't appear in any rate: it's cash in a pocket for the length of a trip.

Working out which route suits a particular trip — against withdrawal charges that scale, spreads that don't publish, and an amount of cash determined by how you travel — is exactly what these guides supply the parts for rather than settle. Turkey, Worked Out settles it.

No. Bringing foreign currency in is free; it's taking cash OUT that must be declared above 10,000 euros equivalent or 185,000 lira. The commonly repeated version has the direction reversed.

Through the spread between their buying and selling rates, with commission practice varying by office. "No commission" describes only one of the two possible charges.

Are airport rates worse than city rates?

No official comparative data exists, so that's folk knowledge rather than a measured fact. Airport exchange does operate under conditions — captive demand, limited competition — that generally shape a spread.

Americans arriving in Turkey encounter a price level that feels improbably low and a currency that behaves in a way most of them have never dealt with. Those two facts are the same fact, and understanding the mechanism explains several things that otherwise look like inconsistency or sharp practice.

The number

Turkey's consumer price index rose 32.11% year-on-year and 0.99% month-on-month in June 2026.

Sit with the first figure. Thirty-two per cent annual consumer inflation is not a statistical abstraction — it means the price of an ordinary basket of goods is roughly a third higher than it was twelve months earlier, in a country where the same basket was already repricing the year before that.

The monthly figure is the more useful one for a traveler, because it describes the pace at which a menu, a hotel rate or a museum ticket becomes out of date.

Why an old figure is a different kind of wrong

Every travel guide carries prices that age. In a low-inflation currency that ageing is slow and roughly uniform — a figure from three years ago is a bit low, and everything is a bit low together.

In this environment the ageing is fast and uneven. A figure from a guide written two years ago isn't slightly low; it may be off by half, and it isn't off by the same proportion as the figure next to it, because different goods reprice at different rates and different times.

That's the structural difference. An old price in a stable currency is an approximation. An old price here is closer to a historical artefact — it tells you what something cost then, and almost nothing about what it costs now.

What repricing looks like on the ground

How often businesses actually revise their prices isn't published, and no official statistic on retail repricing frequency exists. What can be said is what the inflation figures imply: at around one per cent a month in the June measurement, a printed menu is measurably stale within a season.

Which is why so much Turkish pricing is written rather than printed, and why a laminated menu with a sticker over the numbers is a normal sight rather than a suspicious one.

Prices in dollars and euros

Visitors notice that some things — tours, transfers, hotel rooms, balloon flights — are quoted in foreign currency while everything else is in lira. There's a legal framework behind that, and it's not the one people assume.

Under Turkey's currency protection regime, contracts between persons resident in Turkey for the sale of goods, services, real estate, vehicle hire and similar transactions may not be denominated or indexed in foreign currency except in cases the Ministry determines. Tourist-facing retail pricing in practice frequently displays dual figures, while the statutory rule requires lira denomination for domestic resident-to-resident contracts.

So foreign-currency pricing is regulated, and the restriction is aimed at contracts between residents. A transaction involving a visitor sits differently from one between two Turkish parties, which is why dual pricing appears where tourists are and largely doesn't where they aren't.

It also means a business quoting you in dollars isn't necessarily doing something irregular — but it is doing something the law has views about, in a framework built to defend the currency rather than to serve travelers.

What the exchange rate does to all this

The lira's movement against the dollar is published daily by the central bank and moves continuously. No figure appears in this article for that reason: any rate printed here would be wrong within days, and printing it would create exactly the false precision the rest of this piece is about.

What matters structurally is that a traveler is exposed to two moving quantities at once — domestic prices rising in lira, and the lira moving against the dollar. Those can offset each other, compound, or diverge, and the net effect on what a trip costs an American is not readable from either number alone.

That is genuinely unusual. In most destinations one of those two is close to still.

What holds steady

Not everything moves. The shape of Turkish spending is durable even when the numbers aren't: the relative cost of a domestic flight against an intercity bus, a neighbourhood lokanta against a tourist restaurant, a public ferry against a chartered boat. Those relationships persist across repricing in a way absolute figures don't.

Which is why the site's cost guidance is expressed as ranges and tiers rather than as fixed sums, and why a figure's age matters more than its precision.

Reading a trip budget against two moving quantities, and knowing which components hold their shape when the numbers don't, is exactly the reasoning these guides supply the parts for. Turkey, Worked Out assembles it.

Istanbul Airport is one of the largest passenger terminals ever built, and for most Americans on a Turkey trip it is where the transatlantic flight meets the domestic one. That handover has a specific shape — which controls you clear, whether your bag comes with you, and how far you physically walk.

Here's what the process involves. What it doesn't involve is a published number telling you how long it takes, and that turns out to be the most useful thing to know about it.

There is no published minimum connection time

Start here, because it's the fact most travelers assume the opposite of.

Neither Istanbul Airport nor Sabiha Gökçen publishes a minimum connection time on its official transfer pages. Not for international-to-international, not for international-to-domestic, not for domestic-to-international. Figures circulate widely — you'll see sixty minutes, ninety minutes, two and a half hours quoted with confidence — and none of them traces back to the airport operator or the regulator.

Airlines apply their own internal connection minima when they sell a through-ticket, which is a different thing: it's the carrier deciding what it will underwrite, not the airport publishing what the building requires. On separate bookings nobody has made that judgement on your behalf at all.

The international-to-domestic path

International-to-domestic transfer passengers clear passport control and then proceed to the domestic transfer point; on a single ticket baggage is normally transferred, otherwise it must be reclaimed and re-checked.

So this connection always involves entering Turkey. Passport control is unavoidable, because the domestic departure area is landside of the international border. That's true whether or not your bag travels with you.

And when the bag doesn't travel with you, the sequence lengthens considerably: passport control, then the baggage hall, then the wait at the belt, then domestic check-in, then security again. Each step is ordinary; the accumulation is not.

Which way round matters

Domestic-to-international runs the same steps in reverse, with one difference in character: you begin landside and clear outbound passport control, so the queue you meet is an exit queue rather than an entry one. The volumes and the times of day behave differently.

Connecting without entering Turkey

International-to-international transfer passengers remain airside, pass transfer security and proceed to the departure gate without clearing immigration, provided the itinerary is on a single ticket and the passenger holds the documents required for the onward destination.

Two conditions are doing real work in that sentence. Airside transit requires the single ticket — two bookings force you through immigration and the baggage hall regardless of where you're going next. And the documents that matter are the ones for your onward destination, checked before you board.

The building itself

IST is a single main terminal with multiple concourses — A, B, D and F international, G and parts of F domestic — and walking distances between the furthest gates can exceed 20 to 30 minutes.

That's walking time inside one terminal, with no train and no landside movement — before any queue. It is the single component travelers most consistently underestimate, because "same terminal" sounds like proximity and here it isn't.

The airport publishes no official figure for the distance between its furthest gates, so the honest statement is the range above rather than a measurement.

The components, laid out

Whatever your connection, it is built from the same parts, and each one is a real elapsed period:

  • Arrival to passport control — including the walk from a possibly distant gate.
  • Passport control — variable, and busiest when several long-haul arrivals land together.
  • Baggage reclaim — only on separate tickets, and it is the longest single unknown.
  • Domestic check-in and bag drop — with its own cut-off, separate from departure time.
  • Security — again.
  • The walk to the domestic gate — potentially the far end of the building.

None of those has a published duration either. What the airport does document is the sequence, which is why the process is knowable while the timing isn't.

Which of these steps you face depends on how the tickets were bought, covered in through-tickets and separate tickets on a Turkey trip. If your onward flight leaves from the city's other airport, none of this applies and the IST-SAW transfer does instead.

Working out what an unpublished connection time means against an international return that is already booked is exactly the reasoning no single guide can do. Turkey, Worked Out does it.

Driving in Turkey is straightforward for an American in most respects — same side of the road, familiar signage conventions, good highways between the main regions. The parts that catch people out are the ones with numbers attached, and a fair amount of what circulates online is out of date.

Here are the rules as the Turkish authorities publish them, plus the two systems that quietly bill you afterwards.

Speed limits

For passenger cars: 50 km/h in built-up areas, 90 km/h on ordinary intercity roads, 110 km/h on dual carriageways, and 130 km/h on motorways, with some build-operate-transfer motorways posted at 140.

Two of those bands are worth noticing. There's a distinct dual-carriageway limit that sits between the intercity road and the motorway, which many summaries omit entirely — and the motorway limit is higher than the figure most English-language sources quote. The road type determines the limit, so the sign is what governs, not an assumption carried over from another country.

Alcohol

The limit is 0.50 promil for private-car drivers, and 0.20 promil for drivers of commercial vehicles and other non-private categories.

Note that the stricter category is 0.20, not zero — another figure widely reported wrongly. For a visitor in a rental car the 0.50 threshold applies, which is below the level most US states set and low enough that a single drink with a meal is a real calculation rather than a theoretical one.

Belts, phones and child seats

Seatbelts are mandatory for all occupants; mobile phone use while driving is prohibited except hands-free; and child restraints are required for children below a height and weight threshold, with the requirement varying by age and size.

The child-seat detail is the one to confirm directly with the rental company if it applies to you — the requirement is real, but the exact thresholds aren't published in a form that survives being quoted second-hand, and a rental child seat is an item to book rather than assume.

Tolls: the system that bills you later

HGS — the Hızlı Geçiş Sistemi — is Turkey's electronic toll collection system for motorways and bridges. Vehicles carry an HGS sticker linked to a prepaid account, and the toll is deducted automatically as the vehicle passes the plaza.

There are no cash lanes to fall back on. A rental car is normally equipped with a transponder registered to the rental company, which means the tolls you incur are charged onward to you — not paid at the roadside and forgotten.

Where a pass goes unpaid — an insufficient balance, for instance — it becomes a violation passage: the registered owner is notified and must pay the toll plus an administrative charge, with the charge escalating if it goes unsettled.

The grace period and the surcharge aren't published in a form worth quoting, so the honest statement is the mechanism rather than a figure. What matters for a renter is the chain: the notice goes to the registered owner, which is the rental company, which then comes to you.

Fines: the same chain, longer

A traffic or parking fine incurred in a rental car is issued to the vehicle's registered owner — the rental company — which identifies the renter from the rental agreement and passes the fine on, typically adding an administrative fee.

Three consequences follow from that chain, and none of them is obvious at the time.

The delay can be long. A speed camera in Turkey doesn't stop you, and the first you hear of it may be a charge appearing weeks after you've flown home. The administrative fee is the rental company's own, on top of the fine itself. And because the charge arrives after the rental has ended, it lands on whatever card the company holds — which is why the deposit and the card details outlive the trip.

Helmets

Helmets are mandatory for motorcycle and scooter riders and their passengers on all roads. The licence question for two-wheelers is a separate and considerably less settled matter, covered in scooters and ATVs in Turkey.

What the rules don't tell you

Everything above is the published position. What sits alongside it — and what the corpus of Turkish driving advice mostly consists of — is the character of the driving itself: assertive in cities, patient on the coast roads, and unforgiving in Istanbul traffic at any hour.

That's real, and it's also not a rule. The rules are the numbers; the driving is the conditions.

How those numbers interact with a rental contract you didn't write and an insurance policy with its own conditions is the calculation none of these guides makes alone. Turkey, Worked Out makes it.

A minor collision in a rental car is one of those situations where the paperwork created in the first twenty minutes determines what happens over the following six months. In Turkey the process has a specific shape, and one document produced at the roadside turns out to matter a long way downstream.

Here's what the law requires at the scene, and what sits behind it.

At the scene

Turkish law requires stopping the vehicle and securing the scene, providing first aid where needed, and reporting the accident to the police where there are injuries or significant damage. For collisions involving material damage only, the parties may complete a joint accident report — the trafik kazası tespit tutanağı — and move the vehicles.

The split there is the thing to understand. Injuries or serious damage means police. Damage only, with both parties in agreement, means the joint form and clearing the road — the vehicles are not required to stay where they stopped.

That joint report is a standard Turkish document, not an improvised exchange of details. It records the position of the vehicles, the damage, and both parties' accounts, signed by both.

Why the report matters months later

This is the part that connects to something a long way from the roadside.

A travel insurance claim arising from an accident asks for a police report among its documents — and a police report exists only if the police were involved at the time. A joint form completed between two drivers is not the same document.

The insurance side of that is covered in what a US travel policy pays for in Turkey, which sets out the documents a claim needs. What's worth registering here is the sequencing: the decision about which route to take is made at the roadside, in a few minutes, usually by people who have just had a shock — and it is not revisitable afterwards. There is no way to obtain a police report for an accident the police never attended.

The insurance underneath

Compulsory motor third-party liability insurance is required for every vehicle in Turkey. It covers liability for bodily injury and property damage caused to third parties; it does not cover damage to the insured vehicle itself, nor the driver's own injuries.

So in a collision where you're at fault, that policy addresses the other party. It says nothing about the car you're driving, which is the rental company's asset, or about you.

The rental company's damage terms sit on top of that statutory layer — the excess, the waiver, the exclusion list — and those are contractual with no regulated form, as covered in what the law says and what the desk says. Which specific damage falls inside or outside the waiver is a question about your contract, not about Turkish law.

Three separate policies, one collision

It's worth seeing how many instruments a single incident engages, because they answer different questions and none of them covers the others:

  • Compulsory third-party liability — the other party's injury and property.
  • The rental company's damage terms — the car you were driving, subject to an excess and an exclusion list you agreed to.
  • Your own travel policy — your medical costs, and its exclusions apply, including any condition about the licence you held.

A driver can be fully covered on one of those and exposed on another in the same event. The licence condition is the one most likely to bite, because it links back to a document decision made before the trip started — see the guide to the International Driving Permit.

What the scene produces

Whatever route is taken, an accident generates a small set of artefacts that later processes depend on: the joint report or the police record, photographs, the other party's details and insurance information, and the rental company's own notification, which its contract will require within a stated period.

None of those can be reconstructed later from memory. The rental contract's notification clause in particular runs on its own clock, separate from anything the police or an insurer needs.

Deciding which route to take at the roadside — with the downstream consequences in view rather than out of sight — is precisely the reasoning these guides can supply the parts for but not perform. Turkey, Worked Out performs it.

FAQ

Do I have to call the police after a car accident in Turkey?

Where there are injuries or significant damage, yes. For material-damage-only collisions the parties may complete a joint accident report and move the vehicles.

Can I move the cars?

For a damage-only collision handled by the joint report, yes — the vehicles don't have to stay in position. Where police attendance is required, the scene is theirs.

Does the compulsory insurance cover the rental car?

No. It covers injury and property damage caused to third parties, not damage to the insured vehicle or the driver's own injuries. The rental company's damage terms cover the car.

Why does it matter whether police attended?

A travel insurance claim arising from an accident asks for a police report, and that document only exists if the police were involved at the time. A joint form between drivers isn't the same thing, and it can't be converted into one afterwards.

Who do I tell first?

The law's requirements come first — securing the scene, first aid, police where required. The rental company has its own notification clause with its own deadline, which runs separately from anything an insurer needs.

Ask whether you need an International Driving Permit for Turkey and you'll get four different answers depending on who you ask — and all four can be correct at once, because they're answers to four different questions. Turkish law, the rental company, your insurer, and the document itself each have their own position.

Here's what the permit actually is and what Turkish law actually says. The other two answers live elsewhere.

What an IDP is, legally

An International Driving Permit is a certified multilingual translation of a domestic driving licence, issued under the 1949 Geneva or 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic; it is not a standalone driving entitlement and is valid only when accompanied by the domestic licence.

That sentence rules out the two things people most often assume. It is not a licence — it grants no permission you don't already hold. And it is useless on its own: presented without your home licence it is a translation of a document you aren't carrying.

The IDP is valid only when carried together with the valid domestic licence. Both, always, or neither.

Where to get one, and what it costs

Only AAA and the American Automobile Touring Alliance are authorised by the US Department of State to issue an IDP, and the fee is USD 20.

That authorisation matters because the internet is full of sites selling "international driving permits" for considerably more. Anything issued by a body other than those two is not the document the conventions describe.

A US-issued IDP is valid for one year from issue, or until the domestic licence expires if that comes first. It is not renewable — a new application is required — and it may be issued up to six months in advance, by mail from within the United States.

The last clause is the practical constraint: it's a document you obtain before you leave, not one you can arrange once you've arrived and discovered you want it.

What Turkish law actually requires

Turkey is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic, having deposited accession in January 2013 with entry into force a year later, and is also a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention. So the permit is a recognised instrument there.

Recognised, though, is not the same as required.

Foreign visitors may drive in Turkey on a foreign licence for a maximum of six months from the date of entry; after six months a Turkish licence is required.

Turkish law does not mandate an IDP for a US licence holder during that six-month visitor period — the foreign licence itself is recognised for the period. An official Turkish translation requirement applies later and in a different context, not as a general IDP requirement for short-stay foreigners.

That is the legal position, from the Highway Traffic Regulation, and it's more permissive than most travel writing suggests. A US licence is a valid instrument to drive on in Turkey for six months.

The three other answers

Which raises the obvious question: why does everyone tell you to get one?

Because the legal threshold is only one of four, and the other three are set by other people.

  • The rental company can require whatever its contract says. Its requirements are commercial terms, not law, and they vary between companies — covered in what the law says and what the desk says.
  • Your insurer writes its own condition, and where a policy covers driving it typically requires a licence valid for the vehicle class plus compliance with local licensing rules. That's in the activities that void travel insurance in Turkey.
  • A police officer at the roadside is reading a document in an alphabet your licence may not use. The IDP's entire function is being legible.

None of those is the legal requirement, and none of them is bound by it either. A rental desk can insist on a document the law doesn't demand, and it is entitled to.

The six-month clock

One detail worth holding onto for longer trips: the six months runs from the date of entry, not from arrival at a rental desk and not per visit. Anyone spending an extended period in Turkey, or making repeated long stays, is measuring against a clock that started at the border.

Below that horizon the foreign licence stands on its own. Above it, the question stops being about permits and becomes about residency and licence exchange, which is a different subject entirely.

Reconciling four thresholds that don't agree — and deciding what to carry — is the kind of judgement each of these guides deliberately leaves open. Turkey, Worked Out puts them side by side.

FAQ

Do I legally need an IDP to drive in Turkey?

No. Turkish law does not mandate one for a US licence holder within the six-month visitor period; the foreign licence is recognised for that period. A rental company or insurer may still require one.

How long can I drive on my US licence?

Up to six months from the date of entry, after which a Turkish licence is required. The clock starts at the border, not at the rental counter.

Where do I get an IDP and what does it cost?

Only AAA and the American Automobile Touring Alliance are State Department authorised, at USD 20. Other sellers are not issuing the document the conventions describe.

How long is it valid?

One year from issue, or until your licence expires if sooner; not renewable, issuable up to six months ahead, and obtainable by mail from within the US — so it's arranged before departure.
